description: Somos uma equipa formada por António Maurício, Adilson Francisco, Agostinho Mariti e Hilton Diamantino. Participamos neste desafio para aprender, trocar ideias e trabalhar em equipa. Temos interesse por tecnologia, programação e inovação, e queremos transformar ideias em soluções para problemas reais, aprendendo e construindo juntos.
summary:
We developed Missão Orbital, an interactive 3D web game created for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge — Space Mission Design Game. The simulator empowers students and space enthusiasts to design, verify, and pilot a complete space mission end-to-end, directly integrating three official NASA engineering documents: CubeSat 101 (CSLI), Concept Maturity Levels (JPL CML 1–4), and Design and Develop Science Missions (BioNutrients-2).

In the real-time 3D Hangar, players choose destinations (ISS, Moon, Mars, or Europa), assemble scientific instruments, and watch every choice recalculate dry mass, inverse-square solar irradiance (1/r²), Δv via the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, budget, FCC/NOAA spectrum licenses, and 35% JPL margins. During live 3D flight, players manage continuous operations (Science Scan, RF Downlink, and Safe Mode) and confront 3D hazards such as meteoroid swarms and solar storms: right calls evade the threat, while errors cause visible hull damage. With Solo, Training, Sandbox, and Team X (2–4 players) modes, a Design Comparator, and a Mission Certificate, the app makes space systems engineering hands-on and accessible.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Missão Orbital turns space mission formulation and operations into a unified, physics-coupled 3D web game inspired directly by NASA engineering workflows. After an interactive mission briefing website, players enter the simulator across four destinations with increasing engineering difficulty:

1. ISS 408 km LEO (CubeSat & BioNutrients-2 Yeast Study — CSLI / NanoRacks SSOD)

2. Moon / Cislunar Orbit (CML 1–4 Artemis CubeSat / SmallSat)

3. Mars (Planetary Science — 43% solar flux, planetary protection, interplanetary Δv)

4. Europa / Jupiter at 5.2 AU (Deep-space extreme mission — 3.7% solar flux, RTG/massive arrays, planetary protection)

Inside the interactive 3D Hangar, every spacecraft decision visibly alters the 3D craft model and recalculates interconnected system constraints in real time:

- Form factor (1U–6U CubeSat, SmallSat, Flagship) and Aluminum 6061-T6 structure

- Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for total Δv against launch vehicle mass capacity

- Inverse-square solar irradiance drop-off (1/r²) enforcing NASA/JPL Pre-Phase A 35% mass and power margins

- Data volume, RF frequency band licensing (FCC/IARU & NOAA), orbital lifetime / ODAR <25-year reentry compliance, and FY26 budget

- Pre-Flight Verification Lab (CubeSat 101): Remove Before Flight (RBF) pin check, 45-minute RF inhibit, Day-in-the-Life (DITL), TVAC, and vibration environmental tests.

During Live 3D Flight, players switch between four operational modes—Science Scan, RF Downlink, Safe Mode (sun-pointing recharge), and Delta-V Burn—while responding to dynamic in-flight engineering decisions and hazards. When a decision is correct, HUD overlays clear briefly so players watch their spacecraft fly closer toward the target planet and cleanly evade incoming 3D meteoroid swarms; wrong decisions trigger visible 3D hull impact damage, bent solar wings, particle sparks, and integrity warnings.

Key Educational Features & Game Modes

- 4 Playable Modes: Solo Career, Guided Training, Free Sandbox, and Team X (2–4 concurrent players assuming Mission Planner, Systems Engineer, Lead Scientist, and Project Manager roles).

- Design Comparator: Side-by-side comparison table of saved mission architectures to analyze trade-offs across mass, power margin, Δv, and CML maturity.

- Post-Flight Debrief & Certificate: Subsystem scoring (Science, Integrity, Comms, CML), tailored engineering recommendations, printable custom Mission Certificate, built-in NASA Glossary, and bilingual EN/PT switcher.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Students and beginner CubeSat teams rarely have access to an end-to-end tool linking conceptual formulation (CML 1–4) with hardware verification and live orbital operations. Missão Orbital bridges that gap directly in the browser with zero setup or login, helping high schoolers, university students, and hackathon participants internalize real NASA trade-offs through cause-and-effect 3D visualization.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

- Frontend & Simulation Engine: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide Icons, Motion

- 3D WebGL Rendering: Three.js (procedural spacecraft assembly, lit planetary targets, orbital motion, 3D meteoroid hazards, and visual damage states)

- Deployment: Vercel Edge static web hosting

- Bilingual & Hackathon Media Tooling: Python, FFmpeg, and ImageMagick used to assemble the English demonstration slide deck and English-narrated / Portuguese-subtitled 30-second video.

Creativity & Engineering Factors Considered

Rather than presenting multiple-choice trivia on top of static text, every UI choice couples directly to live aerospace equations and 3D scene feedback—removing question cards after right answers to celebrate spacecraft progression toward the target planet and visualizing physical evasion vs. structural failure during space hazards. We also enforced strict planetary protection rules for Mars/Europa, JPL 35% margins, and CubeSat 101 regulatory gates.

Super Intelligence (SI) Transparency Disclosure

Super Intelligence (AI) tools were used to accelerate TypeScript/React/Three.js software development, English translation, text-to-speech English voiceover narration for the demo video, and demo slide/video asset generation. No NASA logos, flags, emblems, or mission insignia were generated or included anywhere in the application, slides, or video, and a visible AI-assistance disclosure badge appears in the presentation and demo video.
